doc.title: Carmen Caramanica interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, July 27, 2011

title: Returning to Utica, teaching commitment and local playing
summary: Teaching since age 14, keeping his studio during Orlando's breaks, and playing selectively locally.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I had moved to Rome and I hadn’t been there that long, and Rick was the first guy I got to know. And I remember when he got that call. He was very excited. And I went over to his house and he was like “I can’t talk to you now, I’ve got this stuff here.” He always had his Fender Rhodes you know. That’s cool. So when you came back here, then you thought well what am I going to do here? Am I going to teach? Was that like forming in your mind, that you could become —

Oh always. When I was in high school I was asked by a music store to do some teaching, and so I’ve been teaching since I was like 14 or 15. You know, after school, there on Saturdays, that kind of stuff. And then even with, well with Lou’s gig somewhat, but I basically shut my studio down for the years I was with Lou. But with Tony’s gig, Tony would work a couple of weeks and then take a couple of weeks off. He had to rest his voice. He didn’t really have a trained singing style. So we’d work two weeks, and then © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -15-

two weeks we didn’t work. And that kind of went on for several years, like clockwork. And so while I was home I would teach. So I kept my studio going and I’d just tell people “okay your next lesson will be such and such a date.” So it was always still there. And I realized that when I would get off the road I could still use that as the basis and do some local playing, and that I did. The local playing scene has gotten leaner and leaner, as you are well aware. But then I spent more of my time concentrating on building my studio.
And now, from my observation, you take this very seriously.
Like, you’re unlikely to cancel a lesson so you can play a gig. Right?

True. Yeah. It’s a commitment to me. I mean not only I feel the students are committed if you schedule lessons with me, you’ve got to be here. You take a class, you make the class. At the same time, if I’m always dumping them because I’ve got a chance to play a gig, that’s not fair to them. Now way way back I used to have certain people come in and sub for me, and say “well you will have a lesson, it’ll be with” so-and-so. And it worked in some cases. In other cases it didn’t work so well and they’d say “well I didn’t really like what this guy did,” or whatever. So I figured okay, if you’re going to have them make a commitment to you, you make a commitment to them.
And I think it works out good locally, it’s like an event when you play out. Well I’m telling you it is.

It’s lucky that it worked out that way, because again, being a burn out, now when I play the gigs that I play now, it’s stuff that I want to play and I enjoy it and it’s great. But it’s nice to have people out there, all right? I remember one time we played this one room, it’s closed now, The Bearded Dolphin. And I think we played it maybe five or six weekends in a row. And the last weekend that we played there there were like two or three guys at the bar watching a basketball game, and the band. That was it. And one of the guys came over and said “do you want to hold it down, we’re trying to watch the game.” And we said we’re playing too much. People aren’t coming out. So we made a conscious decision to only play once every eight or ten weeks or something like that, so we really would enjoy what we were doing and maybe people will come. And that’s worked out very well for us. When we do play we get a decent sized audience, and we look forward to the next gig rather than saying “are you ready to do it again, and again, and again.” Maybe it shouldn’t be that way but it is for me. If I’ve got to play five nights a week again, no matter what I’m playing, I don’t know if I’d like that as much.
